blocks.html: In a distributed system, multiple nodes (servers, databases, replicas) often need to agree on committing a transaction simultaneously.
blocks.text: In a distributed system, multiple nodes (servers, databases, replicas) often need to agree on committing a transaction simultaneously.

blocks.html: If all commit together → system stays consistent.
blocks.text: If all commit together → system stays consistent.

blocks.html: If one commits but the other does not → inconsistency occurs.
blocks.text: If one commits but the other does not → inconsistency occurs.

blocks.html: The problem: messages between nodes can get lost, delayed, or fail.
blocks.text: The problem: messages between nodes can get lost, delayed, or fail.

blocks.html: Because of this, no node can ever be 100% certain that the other node received its decision.
blocks.text: Because of this, no node can ever be 100% certain that the other node received its decision.

blocks.html: Node A wants to update x = 10:

A temporarily sets
x = 10
(but doesn't commit yet)

blocks.html: A sends message to B: "Let's both update x = 10"

B temporarily sets

blocks.html:
B thinks: "What if my reply gets lost? Then A won't know I'm ready, and A will rollback to
x = 0
"
blocks.text: B thinks: "What if my reply gets lost? Then A won't know I'm ready, and A will rollback to x = 0"

blocks.html: B sends back: "OK, I'm ready to update x = 10"
blocks.text: B sends back: "OK, I'm ready to update x = 10"

blocks.html: The problem begins:
blocks.text: The problem begins:

blocks.html:
Even if A gets B's reply, A thinks: "But what if B doesn't know I received the reply? B might think I rolled back and B will also rollback to
x = 0
"
blocks.text: Even if A gets B's reply, A thinks: "But what if B doesn't know I received the reply? B might think I rolled back and B will also rollback to x = 0"

blocks.html: So A sends: "Got your reply! Let's commit x = 10"
blocks.text: So A sends: "Got your reply! Let's commit x = 10"

blocks.html: It never ends:
blocks.text: It never ends:

blocks.html: Now B thinks: "Did A get my confirmation? What if A thinks I rolled back?"
blocks.text: Now B thinks: "Did A get my confirmation? What if A thinks I rolled back?"

blocks.html: B sends: "Got your confirmation! Really committing x = 10"
blocks.text: B sends: "Got your confirmation! Really committing x = 10"

blocks.html: This continues forever...
blocks.text: This continues forever...

blocks.html:
The result: Neither node can ever be 100% certain the other will commit. They're stuck in an endless loop of confirmations, never able to safely update
x
from 0 to 10.

blocks.html: Solution?
blocks.text: Solution?

blocks.html: There is no perfect solution to the Two Generals’ Problem. Here’s why:
blocks.text: There is no perfect solution to the Two Generals’ Problem. Here’s why:

blocks.html: The core issue is unreliable communication. No matter how many acknowledgements are exchanged, there is always uncertainty about whether the last message was received.
blocks.text: The core issue is unreliable communication. No matter how many acknowledgements are exchanged, there is always uncertainty about whether the last message was received.

blocks.html: This makes absolute agreement impossible to guarantee.
blocks.text: This makes absolute agreement impossible to guarantee.

blocks.html: The problem has been formally proven unsolvable in distributed systems theory.
blocks.text: The problem has been formally proven unsolvable in distributed systems theory.

blocks.html: The uncertainty cannot be eliminated with any finite number of messages.
blocks.text: The uncertainty cannot be eliminated with any finite number of messages.

blocks.html: In real systems, protocols like Two-Phase Commit (2PC) or Three-Phase Commit (3PC) are used.
blocks.text: In real systems, protocols like Two-Phase Commit (2PC) or Three-Phase Commit (3PC) are used.

blocks.html: These do not solve the problem perfectly but reduce uncertainty with assumptions such as reliable channels, timeouts, and failure detectors.
blocks.text: These do not solve the problem perfectly but reduce uncertainty with assumptions such as reliable channels, timeouts, and failure detectors.

blocks.html: A perfect solution that always works under all conditions does not exist.
blocks.text: A perfect solution that always works under all conditions does not exist.

blocks.html: What exists are practical protocols that work well enough in real-world networks but rely on assumptions, so they are not truly perfect.
blocks.text: What exists are practical protocols that work well enough in real-world networks but rely on assumptions, so they are not truly perfect.
